meta.title: Who really said "It is utterly false and cruelly arbitrary to put all the play and learning into childhood, all the work into middle age, and all the regrets into old age"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Credited to Margaret Mead, but the only citation is a 1958 teachers' anthology quoting her second-hand. No source in her own work has ever been produced.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'It is utterly false and cruelly arbitrary to put all the play and learning into childhood, all the work into middle age, and all the regrets into old age'?
meta.ogDescription: Attributed to Margaret Mead. Traced only to a 1958 anthology that quotes her second-hand - and the popular version quietly closes an ellipsis.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Credited to Mead everywhere the line appears, and consistent with the subjects she built a career on — childhood, the life cycle, how people are raised and educated. But the only citation anyone attaches to it is a 1958 teachers’ anthology that prints it second-hand; no book, article, lecture, column or interview of Mead’s own has been shown to contain it, and the version that circulates online quietly closes an ellipsis the documented text carries.

source.excerpt: It is utterly false and cruelly arbitrary… to put all the play and learning into childhood, all the work into middle age, and all the regrets into old age.
trail: Wikiquote ↗ places the line among Mead’s 1950s quotations with a single citation: “As quoted in Teacher’s Treasury of Stories for Every Occasion (1958) by Millard Dale Baughman, p. 69.” The phrase “as quoted in” is doing the work here — it flags a second-hand source, not a Mead publication, and Wikiquote offers nothing earlier.

That anthology is real and datable: Open Library ↗ and Google Books ↗ both record it as Millard Dale Baughman, Prentice-Hall, 1958, 375 pages — a compilation of anecdotes and quotations assembled for teachers to use in talks. Books of that kind reprint sayings without naming where they came from.

No specialist verdict exists to defer to. Quote Investigator’s Mead file ↗ covers three other attributions — “Never doubt that a small group…”, “Always remember that you are absolutely unique…”, and the healed-femur anecdote — but has never examined this sentence.

The line has not been located in Mead’s own corpus in the course of this check, and no other author has ever been proposed for it. That combination — one consistent name, one second-hand citation, no primary text — is what “attributed” means.
source.excerptNote: This is the wording as Wikiquote’s sourced entry records it, ellipsis included — that gap marks words omitted from whatever Mead originally said, and the anthology does not say what they were. The familiar internet version silently closes it.

source.rightsHolder: The Estate of Margaret Mead; Prentice-Hall (publisher of the 1958 anthology)
source.rightsNote: The earliest printing on record for this wording is Teacher’s Treasury of Stories for Every Occasion, published by Prentice-Hall in 1958 — so it is potentially still protected, though US works of that period entered the public domain unless the copyright was renewed in its twenty-eighth year, and no renewal search for this title has been made. The text is nonetheless treated as in‑copyright on the stronger ground: the underlying Mead source has not been identified, so its own publication date and rights position are unknown, and any Mead statement of the 1950s would be modern, copyrighted material. Nothing here supports a public-domain claim.

author.name: Margaret Mead
author.heading: Who Margaret Mead was
author.metaLine: 1901–1978 · American cultural anthropologist and museum curator
author.bio: Margaret Mead (born 16 December 1901, died 15 November 1978) was the best-known American anthropologist of the twentieth century — curator of ethnology at the American Museum of Natural History from 1946 to 1969, an adjunct professor at Columbia, and later president of the American Association for the Advancement of Science. Her research concentrated on childhood, adolescence, sexuality and kinship, beginning with Coming of Age in Samoa (1928), and she spent decades explaining to general readers how cultures raise and educate their young — including a long-running monthly column in Redbook co-authored with Rhoda Métraux. That public-intellectual reach is exactly why so many unsourced aphorisms about children, ageing and social change ended up with her name on them.

misattribution.heading: What gets it wrong
misattribution.intro: No rival author has ever claimed this line, so the problem here is not the wrong name — it is false precision. Quote sites present a second-hand anthology entry as if it were a Mead publication, and they present a smoothed sentence as if it were her exact words.

items.who: The ellipsis-free version that circulates online
items.why: The documented text runs “It is utterly false and cruelly arbitrary… to put all the play and learning into childhood” — the ellipsis is part of Wikiquote’s sourced entry ↗, marking words dropped from whatever Mead actually said. Every popular rendering deletes it and closes the gap, turning an already-abridged quotation into a clean sentence nobody can prove she uttered.

items.who: Goodreads, BrainyQuote and the wider quote-site layer
items.why: Goodreads prints it as one unbroken sentence ↗ credited to Margaret Mead with no source book, date or occasion at all. That is how a second-hand anthology entry becomes, in a few reposts, an apparent quotation from Mead’s own writing.

items.who: Margaret Mead as a quotation magnet
items.why: Wikiquote keeps a whole Disputed section for her, and Quote Investigator has published on three separate Mead attributions — concluding of the most famous that researchers could not find it in her corpus ↗, and tracing the “healed femur” story to a single 1980 recollection ↗. Her name attracts wise-sounding lines; assume nothing about a Mead quote until it is cited.

misattribution.truthLine: What is actually documented: the sentence is credited to Margaret Mead in Millard Dale Baughman’s Teacher’s Treasury of Stories for Every Occasion (Prentice-Hall, 1958) ↗, page 69 — an anthology quoting her, published while she was alive, with an ellipsis in the middle and no underlying source named. Nobody has found the Mead text it came from.

context.heading: Why this one is hard to pin down
lead: The sentence is a small piece of social criticism: it argues that the standard Western life script — learn, then work, then regret — is not a fact of nature but a choice, and a bad one. That argument sits squarely inside Mead’s public work. She spent her career on childhood, adolescence, kinship and how cultures raise and educate their young ↗, and she made those arguments in lecture halls, magazine columns and radio far more than in footnoted monographs.

That is precisely the problem. A line delivered from a podium or dropped into a magazine answer column can be copied into an anthology, credited correctly, and still leave no citable trail back to a Mead text. The oldest citation on this quote — a 1958 book of anecdotes compiled for teachers to use in speeches — is the kind of source that records that she said something without recording where.
detailsBody: A dated appearance in one of Mead’s own books, in her Redbook column, in a conference proceeding, or in a contemporary newspaper report that names the occasion would move this to verified. So would the entry in the 1958 anthology itself if, as some compilations do, it names the magazine or address it was lifted from — page 69 of that book has not been examined here.

Until then the honest statement is the narrow one: Margaret Mead is the only person the line has ever been credited to, the credit goes back at least to a book published while she was alive and internationally famous, and no one has produced the underlying source.
context.pull: Attributed is not the same as verified — and the difference is a footnote nobody ever wrote down.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote lists the quote in Margaret Mead's 1950s (sourced) section with the wording 'It is utterly false and cruelly arbitrary... to put all the play and learning into childhood, all the work into middle age, and all the regrets into old age.' cited 'As quoted in Teacher's Treasury of Stories for Every Occasion (1958) by Millard Dale Baughman, p. 69'; the page also has a separate Disputed section covering 'Never doubt that a small group...', 'Always remember that you are absolutely unique...' and the healed-femur anecdote.

Open Library records 'Teacher's treasury of stories for every occasion' by Millard Dale Baughman, Prentice-Hall, Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey, 1958, 375 pages, described as a collection of anecdotes, aphorisms and quotations.
Google Books records the title 'Teacher's Treasury of Stories for Every Occasion' by Millard Dale Baughman, publisher Prentice-Hall, published 1958, 375 pages.
Goodreads displays the quote as one unbroken sentence with no ellipsis, attributed to Margaret Mead, with no source book, date or citation given.

Quote Investigator's Margaret Mead results cover three attributions - the healed femur, 'Never doubt that a small group of thoughtful, committed citizens can change the world', and 'Always remember that you are absolutely unique' - and include no article on 'It is utterly false and cruelly arbitrary to put all the play and learning into childhood'.

Quote Investigator states that researchers have been unsuccessful in finding the 'Never doubt that a small group of thoughtful, committed citizens can change the world' quotation in Margaret Mead's corpus.

Quote Investigator finds no direct evidence from Margaret Mead for the 'healed femur is the earliest sign of civilization' anecdote and traces it to surgeon Paul Brand's 1980 recollection of a lecture.

Wikipedia gives Margaret Mead's dates as December 16, 1901 - November 15, 1978, describes her as a cultural anthropologist and curator of ethnology at the American Museum of Natural History (1946-1969) and adjunct professor at Columbia, notes her research concentrated on childhood, adolescence, sexuality and kinship, lists Coming of Age in Samoa (1928), and records her monthly Redbook column co-authored with Rhoda Metraux.
